title: Proverbs 8:22–31
context: Wisdom speaks of her origin before creation. The LORD possessed her at the beginning of his work. She was set up from everlasting and brought forth before the depths, springs, mountains, and earth. She was present as he established the heavens, marked the horizon, set the clouds, bounded the sea, and laid earth’s foundations. She was beside him as craftsman, delighting before him and rejoicing in his world and in humanity. This passage is a major interpretive crux. It has been read as a poetic personification of God’s wisdom and, in Christian tradition, in connection with Christ, whom the New Testament calls the wisdom of God. Its key words have been understood in more than one way.

verses.text: “The LORD possessed me in the beginning of his work, before his deeds of old.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD possessed me in the beginning of his work. The Hebrew verb qanah can mean possess, acquire, create, or beget, and translations differ; the Greek Septuagint used a verb meaning created. Many read the passage as poetic personification: wisdom is God’s own attribute, so it is as old as God’s work. Arminian and Reformed readers alike share the historic Christian rejection of any reading that makes Christ a creature.
verses.reformedNotes: Christian readers historically linked this passage with Christ, the wisdom of God, as 1 Corinthians 1:24 says. In the fourth century Arius cited this verse for a created Son. Athanasius and the Nicene tradition answered by applying it to the incarnation or reading it in other ways. Reformed readers stand with Nicene orthodoxy, as Arminians do. Some apply the verse to Christ, while others take it as personified wisdom and draw on it only by analogy.

verses.text: I was set up from everlasting, from the beginning, before the earth existed.
verses.arminianNotes: I was set up from everlasting, before the earth existed. Arminian readers see wisdom as prior to creation, which means God’s works are planned in wisdom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see wisdom’s antiquity before creation. Those reading christologically connect it to the Son’s eternal existence, as John 1:1 and Micah 5:2 say.

verses.text: When there were no depths, I was born, when there were no springs abounding with water.
verses.arminianNotes: When there were no depths, I was born. The verb means brought forth, a birth image. Arminian readers note the poetic picture rather than a technical claim about origins.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers who read the passage christologically connect the birth language with the doctrine of the Son’s eternal generation, while recognizing that the poetry is not a technical statement.

verses.text: Before the mountains were settled in place, before the hills, I was born;
verses.arminianNotes: Before the mountains were settled in place, I was born. Arminian readers see the repetition stressing wisdom’s priority to the oldest things of creation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the emphasis on wisdom’s precedence, which Psalm 90:2 applies to God himself. The language stresses that wisdom was already present before the oldest parts of the created world.

verses.text: while as yet he had not made the earth, nor the fields, nor the beginning of the dust of the world.
verses.arminianNotes: Before he made the earth or the fields or the first dust of the world. Arminian readers see creation itself as the product of prior wisdom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress God’s decree and wisdom preceding creation. God did not improvise creation; everything was made according to his wise counsel, as Ephesians 1:11 reflects.

verses.text: When he established the heavens, I was there. When he set a circle on the surface of the deep,
verses.arminianNotes: When he established the heavens I was there; when he set a circle on the face of the deep. Arminian readers see wisdom as witness to creation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see creation as an act of God’s wisdom, as Psalm 104:24 says, and some connect this with the Son as agent of creation in Colossians 1:16.

verses.text: when he established the clouds above, when the springs of the deep became strong,
verses.arminianNotes: When he established the clouds and the springs of the deep. Arminian readers see God’s orderly design throughout creation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see providence and creation ordered by wisdom. Clouds and springs alike are set in place by design, not chance.

verses.text: when he gave to the sea its boundary, that the waters should not violate his commandment, when he marked out the foundations of the earth,
verses.arminianNotes: When he gave the sea its boundary and marked the earth’s foundations. Arminian readers see God setting limits on chaos, as in Job 38:8–11.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s sovereign command over the sea, which obeys his word. The boundaries of the sea display a Creator who restrains chaos by command, a theme the Psalms celebrate.

verses.text: then I was the craftsman by his side. I was a delight day by day, always rejoicing before him,
verses.arminianNotes: Then I was the craftsman by his side. The Hebrew word amon is debated: it may mean master craftsman, or nursling or little child, which fits the delight and play language. Arminian readers note both options and the joy in creation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise acknowledge the debate. Those reading christologically connect the craftsman sense with the Son as agent of creation and the delight with the Father’s love for the Son.

verses.text: rejoicing in his whole world. My delight was with the sons of men.
verses.arminianNotes: Rejoicing in his whole world; my delight was with the sons of men. Arminian readers see wisdom’s delight in humanity, which reflects God’s love for people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s delight in humanity. Those reading christologically see the Son’s love for humanity anticipating the incarnation.
